Physical Therapist Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A physical therapist resume has to prove two things in seconds. First, that you are licensed and trained for the setting: DPT, state license, and the board certification that matches the caseload. Second, that your patients actually got better — measured, not claimed. A resume that lists techniques without outcomes reads like a course catalogue. One that pairs each technique with a result reads like a clinician.

This guide gives you a full annotated example from an outpatient orthopedic clinic, a section-by-section breakdown, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you did, at what volume, and with what result.

Quick answer: A physical therapist resume should include a summary naming your DPT degree, state license, and setting; a clinical block with your caseload, the techniques you use, and the outcome measures you track; a certifications block with board specialties; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or functional gains achieved.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with license and setting — DPT, state license, and the clinic type and caseload you treat.
  • Prove outcomes with named measures: Oswestry, DASH, or LEFS scores, with the change you achieved.
  • Name the techniques you actually use: manual therapy, therapeutic exercise, gait training, dry needling.
  • Every experience bullet pairs a duty with a count: patients per day, visits per week, or goals met at discharge.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Clinic Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a clinic director and you will not hear “passionate about helping people.” You will hear:

  • License, stated plainly. DPT and the state license, with the board certification that matches the caseload — OCS for orthopedics, SCS for sports. An unlicensed applicant goes in a different pile.
  • Caseload volume. Patients per day, visits per week, and the mix: post-operative, chronic pain, sports injuries. A therapist who carries 14 patients a day in a busy outpatient clinic is a safer hire than one who lists techniques without numbers.
  • Measured outcomes. Oswestry, DASH, or LEFS scores with the change achieved, and the share of patients discharged meeting their goals.
  • Documentation fluency. WebPT, Clinicient, or Epic, named exactly. Notes are half the job, and a hire who needs weeks of training costs the clinic a month of productivity.
  • Retention and reliability. No-show rates managed down, schedules kept full, and patients who finish their plan of care.

If your resume reads like a duties list — all responsibilities, no volumes — it will lose to one that reads like a caseload record.

Physical Therapist Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is a complete example from an outpatient orthopedic clinic. It’s fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you did, the volume, and the result.

DANIEL OKAFOR, DPT, OCS
Austin, TX · (512) 555-0147 · daniel.okafor@email.com

SUMMARY
Licensed Physical Therapist (DPT, OCS) with 6 years in outpatient orthopedics, including 4 years at a 5-clinician clinic treating 65 visits a week. Carry 14 patients a day across post-operative, sports, and chronic-pain caseloads; 9 in 10 patients discharged meeting their goals. Dry needling certified; BLS current.

LICENSE & CERTIFICATIONS
Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) · Licensed Physical Therapist, Texas · Board Certified Orthopaedic Clinical Specialist (OCS) · Dry Needling Certification · Basic Life Support (BLS), current

SKILLS
Manual therapy · Therapeutic exercise · Gait training · Neuromuscular re-education · Dry needling · Post-operative rehabilitation · Sports injury rehabilitation · Chronic pain management · Outcome measurement · WebPT · Patient education · Home exercise programs

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Physical Therapist — Hill Country Orthopedic Physical Therapy, Austin, TX | 2021–Present

  • Treat 14 patients a day in a 5-clinician outpatient clinic across post-operative, sports, and chronic-pain caseloads
  • Cut average Oswestry Disability Index scores from 42 to 18 across a 10-visit episode for lower-back patients, with 9 in 10 discharged meeting their goals
  • Built the clinic’s return-to-sport testing protocol, clearing 30+ athletes a year back to full play with no re-injury in 3 months
  • Cut the no-show rate from 12% to 6% by tightening reminders and filling cancelled slots from the waitlist the same day
  • Keep WebPT notes current with same-day documentation across a 65-visit week

Physical Therapist — Riverside Sports Medicine, Austin, TX | 2019–2021

  • Treated 12 patients a day in a sports-medicine clinic, including high-school and college athletes across 8 sports
  • Ran the ACL rehabilitation program, returning 25 athletes to full competition over 2 seasons with strength symmetry above 90%
  • Designed home exercise programs for every patient, lifting plan-of-care completion from 7 in 10 to 9 in 10
  • Trained 3 new graduates on manual therapy technique, gait assessment, and WebPT documentation

Clinical Rotation — St. David’s Rehabilitation Hospital, Austin, TX | 2019 (14 weeks)

  • Completed a 14-week inpatient rehab rotation, treating 8 patients a day across stroke, spinal cord, and post-surgical caseloads
  • Tracked LEFS and gait-speed measures on every patient, presenting weekly outcome summaries to the supervising therapist

EDUCATION
Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) — Texas State University, 2019 · BS Kinesiology, University of Texas at Austin, 2016

Why it works: the summary leads with the license and the two numbers clinics check — patients per day and goals met at discharge. Every bullet pairs a duty with a count, and the climb from rotation to a 5-clinician clinic shows the progression.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: license and setting first, then outcomes

“DPT, OCS,” “5-clinician clinic,” “14 patients a day,” “9 in 10 discharged meeting their goals” — the license answers the eligibility question; the outcomes answer the competence question.

Experience: volumes and measures, not responsibilities

“Provided physical therapy services” is a responsibility; “cut Oswestry scores from 42 to 18 across a 10-visit episode” is proof of clinical effect. The strongest bullets show a measure that moved because of work you did.

Certifications: exact letters, current status

List the credential exactly as it appears on the certificate, with the state license and board specialty up front. Hiring managers screen on these letters before reading experience.

Physical Therapist Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s language exactly: “manual therapy” vs “hands-on treatment” matters:

  • Clinical: manual therapy, therapeutic exercise, gait training, neuromuscular re-education, dry needling, post-operative rehabilitation, sports injury rehabilitation, chronic pain management, balance training, vestibular rehabilitation
  • Assessment: outcome measures, Oswestry Disability Index, DASH, LEFS, gait analysis, range of motion, strength testing, functional movement screening
  • Systems: WebPT, Clinicient, Epic, electronic medical record, EMR, documentation, plan of care, home exercise program
  • Credentials: DPT, licensed physical therapist, OCS, SCS, NCS, board certified, BLS, CPR, dry needling certification

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Clinics screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template in Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for physical therapists. Note the difference from the medical assistant role: medical assistants work under a physician across clinical and administrative tasks, while physical therapists evaluate patients and own the plan of care.

5 Mistakes That Cost Physical Therapists Interviews

  1. Hiding the license. A resume that buries DPT and the state license at the bottom forces the reader to hunt for the two lines that decide the pile. Put them in the summary and in their own block.
  2. Listing techniques instead of outcomes. “Manual therapy and therapeutic exercise” is a course list; “Oswestry scores from 42 to 18 across a 10-visit episode” is clinical effect. Lead with outcomes.
  3. Claiming a credential you do not hold. “OCS” when you have never sat the board exam is a misrepresentation clinics verify. State it honestly: “OCS candidate” or “board exam scheduled.”
  4. No documentation system named. WebPT, Clinicient, or Epic — a resume without a system reads as if notes were never done. Name the system and the years you used it.
  5. One generic resume for every setting. Tailor the summary and first bullets to the setting: volume and return-to-sport speed for sports medicine, outcome measures for outpatient orthopedics, patience and repetition for inpatient rehab.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a physical therapist resume?

A summary naming your DPT degree, state license, and setting; a clinical block with your caseload, the techniques you use, and the outcome measures you track; a certifications block with board specialties such as OCS; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or functional gains achieved.

How do I show patient outcomes on a physical therapist resume?

Name the outcome measure and the change: Oswestry Disability Index scores down from 42 to 18, DASH scores improved by 25 points, or 9 in 10 patients discharged meeting their goals. Pair each measure with the setting and the episode length, because a number without context reads as a guess.

What certifications should a physical therapist list on a resume?

List the ones you actually hold: your DPT and state license first, then board certifications such as OCS for orthopedics or SCS for sports, plus BLS or CPR and technique credentials like dry needling or manual therapy where you have them. Never claim a credential you do not hold; clinics verify licenses before the first shift.

How long should a physical therapist resume be?

One page for most physical therapists, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a career across genuinely different settings, such as outpatient orthopedics, hospital rehab, and home health, that each need space; even then keep the license, the strongest outcomes, and the board certification on page one.

What is the difference between a physical therapist and a physical therapist assistant on a resume?

A physical therapist evaluates patients, diagnoses movement dysfunction, and owns the plan of care. A physical therapist assistant implements that plan under the therapist's supervision. State the scope you actually held, and never claim evaluations or plans of care you did not own.

Do I need experience to get a physical therapist job?

Most clinics hire new graduates, especially from a strong clinical rotation. A rotation counts as experience if you name the setting, the weeks, the caseload, and the outcome measures you used: patients treated per day, techniques applied, and goals met. Lead with the rotation and the license, not with unrelated jobs.
